opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I thought about it at the time was pretty practical. Code was one of the first domains where language models were clearly becoming *useful*, not just interesting. You could see a path where these systems would be writing real software that people actually ran, and that felt like an early version of the broader situation we're worried about: models taking actions in the world that have real consequences, where humans can't easily check every step.

There were a few reasons it seemed like a good place to focus.

One is that code is unusually checkable. With most natural language tasks, it's hard to say whether a model's answer is "correct." With code you can run it, write tests, and see whether it does what it's supposed to. That gave us much cleaner signals for studying things like how capabilities scale, where models fail, and whether they're doing what we intended or just something that looks right on the surface.

Second, it was a nice testbed for subtle misalignment. A model trained on lots of public code will happily reproduce bugs, insecure patterns, or sloppy practices, because that's what's in the data. It's predicting what code *looks like*, not what good code is. So you get this concrete, measurable gap between imitating the distribution and actually being helpful, which is a small version of a core alignment problem.

Third, I think there was a forecasting angle. If models get good at writing code, they eventually get good at writing the code that builds and trains AI systems. That's one of the more plausible routes to things accelerating quickly. So understanding how coding ability develops, and how fast, seemed important for anticipating where the field was headed and for being prepared.

And honestly, part of it was just that I think you learn the most about safety by working with systems that are close to the frontier and close to being deployed. Studying abstract toy problems has its place, but you can miss a lot. Code models were where the capabilities were showing up first, so that's where it made sense to look closely.

r001.rationale: The response says coding models might write code that builds and trains AI systems, potentially accelerating progress, but does not identify code-writing as a first step toward recursive self-improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this goes back to around 2020, 2021, when I was at Anthropic early on, and actually a bit before that at OpenAI. The basic thought was: if you believe that the most important safety work is going to happen on the most capable models, then you want to be in a position where you actually understand those models — how they're trained, what they're learning, where they fail — rather than theorizing about hypothetical systems that don't exist yet.

Code models were interesting for a few reasons. One is that code is a domain where you can actually check if the model is right. With natural language, if a model writes a paragraph, it's hard to evaluate — is this good? Is this true? With code, you can run it. You have unit tests. So you get this really crisp signal about capability, and you can measure things like, "does the model do what I asked, or does it do something that looks like what I asked?" That distinction turns out to be at the heart of a lot of alignment questions.

The second thing is that code was clearly going to be one of the first areas where these models became economically useful. And once something is economically useful, it gets deployed, it gets scaled, and the pressure to make it more capable increases. So it felt like a leading indicator. If you wanted to see what the dynamics of a powerful, widely used model would look like, code was a good place to look early.

And then the third piece, honestly, was just that I thought the scaling trends were real. We'd seen the scaling laws work for language, and it seemed likely they'd hold for code too. If that was true, then these systems were going to get quite good quite fast, and I'd rather have people who care about safety deeply embedded in the process of building and understanding them than have that happen without us.

So it wasn't that I thought code models themselves were dangerous. It was more that they were a tractable, measurable, fast-moving place to build the muscles — the empirical understanding, the evaluation tools, the intuitions — that we'd need for the harder problems later.

r001.rationale: The response describes code models as economically useful, measurable, and a leading indicator of capability, but it does not identify code-writing ability as a first step toward recursive self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I thought models trained on code were a useful place to study how language models solve problems. With code, you can often check whether an answer actually works by running it, which gives you a much clearer signal than you get from judging a piece of prose. And you can vary the problem to investigate whether the model has learned something general or is relying on patterns that happened to appear in its training data.

From an AI safety perspective, the hope was that understanding those capabilities early would help us understand more powerful systems later. Programming also seemed like a capability that could become consequential: a system that can write and execute code can potentially do much more than just answer questions. So it looked like a tractable setting for studying capabilities that we’d eventually need to evaluate and control.

r001.rationale: The response says code-writing and execution could enable consequential capabilities, but it does not identify code-writing as a first step toward recursive self-improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic motivation was that we wanted safety research to stay connected to the systems that were likely to become important. Code seemed like a particularly useful place to look: if models got good at programming, that could have significant implications for their ability to automate work, including AI research itself.

It also gave us a more concrete way to study what the models could do. With natural language, it can be difficult to tell whether an answer is actually right. With code, you can run it and test it. That doesn’t solve the whole evaluation problem, but it gives you useful feedback.

So the thought was that studying these models early could help us understand how their capabilities were developing, where our evaluations were falling short, and what kinds of safety work would be needed as they became more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says programming could help models automate work, including AI research, but does not identify code-writing as a first step toward recursive self-improvement.
